evidence.finding: Voice-platform monitoring reported intermittent call-processing delays across all queues at 09:15, coincident with the start of the severe degradation.
Aggregate service level fell from 77.38% at 09:00 to 34.78% at 09:15 and remained between 16.25% and 46.88% through 11:45.
ASA increased from 42.3 seconds at 09:00 to 96.3 seconds at 09:15, subsequently reaching 148.0 seconds.
At 09:15 only 48 of 73 offered calls were answered and 25 abandoned; abandonment remained between 19 and 42 calls per interval afterward, indicating sustained queue growth and reduced throughput.
Scheduled and logged-in staffing remained constant at 49 agents, while productive staffing remained stable at 44–46 agents throughout the window.
Demand around the onset was not a surge: 73 calls were offered against 79 forecast at 09:15, followed by 67 against 79 at 09:30 and 76 against 79 at 09:45.
Several later intervals exceeded forecast moderately, including 88 versus 75 calls at 11:00 and 87 versus 72 at 11:30, which likely aggravated recovery but does not explain the onset.
All major queues experienced degradation after 09:15, while interval severity varied by queue; this is consistent with an all-queue platform disruption interacting with local workload differences.

primary_root_cause_detail: An all-queue voice-platform degradation reported at 09:15 caused intermittent call-processing delays, reducing answer throughput and producing sustained queueing, high abandonment, elevated ASA, and severe service-level degradation despite stable staffing, AHT, and transfer rates.
recommended_actions: Engage the voice-platform owner to isolate and remediate the source of the intermittent processing delays and confirm full recovery across every queue.
Correlate platform latency, call setup, media-processing, and error telemetry with the 09:15–11:45 interval and preserve logs for root-cause analysis.
Validate failover and redundancy behavior, and define automated mitigation or traffic-diversion thresholds for future all-queue processing degradation.
After platform recovery, monitor ASA, abandonment, answer throughput, and queue depth until backlogs clear; use temporary overflow capacity if required.
Review the moderate late-window volume increases when sizing recovery capacity, while retaining the platform incident as the primary cause.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Offered volume was below forecast at the 09:15 onset and in several subsequent intervals; later moderate increases could worsen queues but cannot explain the abrupt all-queue degradation.
All 49 scheduled agents remained logged in, with productive staffing stable at 44–46 and above forecast requirements of 36–39.
Adherence remained stable at approximately 89.8%–93.9% and improved later in the incident.
Aggregate AHT remained near its forecast range and did not increase at onset; it fell from 382.8 seconds at 09:00 to 371.7 seconds at 09:15.
No routing-change event is supplied, and the documented event identifies platform-wide processing delays rather than a routing modification.
Queue outcomes diverged, but staffing by queue remained unchanged and degradation became broad across queues, making imbalance an effect or local amplifier rather than the primary cause.
Forecast demand and AHT were broadly aligned with actual conditions at onset, while severe degradation occurred even when offered calls were below forecast.
Aggregate service level recalculates according to the supplied definition, and offered calls consistently equal answered plus abandoned calls.

stakeholder_summary: CC-009 was primarily caused by a confirmed all-queue voice-platform degradation beginning at 09:15. Call-processing delays reduced throughput and drove sustained queues, high abandonment, ASA up to 148 seconds, and service levels as low as 16.25%. Staffing, adherence, AHT, and transfer behavior were stable, and demand was below forecast at onset. Moderate later volume increases aggravated recovery but were not the initiating cause.
